newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to review immigration laws-Jospin.
newsitem.headline: France to review immigration laws-Jospin.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday he would review France's hardline laws on immigration and restore the right for anyone born on French soil to French citizenship.

"The legislation on citizenship, foreigners and immigration which was made complex and at times incoherent through too many successive changes, will be reviewed as a whole," he said in his first policy statement to the National Assembly.
"A bill will be tabled during the next parliamentary session," he said.

Jospin said he would restore the right to French citizenship for anyone born in France, which had been partially abolished by the previous conservative government as part of tough laws to curb immigration.

"...The right of soil is consubstantial to the French nation. We will restore it," he said. In a break with French tradition, the previous government had made it necessary for children of foreigners born in France to request citizenship.
Jospin said his leftwing government would keep fighting illegal immigration and clandestine labour but would look into "intolerable" individual situations.

Keeping an election campaign promise, he has already appointed a mediator to oversee a case-by-case review of tens of thousands of illegal immigrants and grant permits to those fulfilling at least one of six criteria set by the National Consultative Council on Human Rights, a civil rights watchdog.

Those who will get residency include parents of children born in France, spouses of immigrants with legal status, those in danger if sent home, patients receiving intensive medical care, students and immigrants "well-integrated in French society".
The move could affect 20,000 to 40,000. A spokesman for the protesters said it could affect 100,000.

Former interior minister Jean-Louis Debre, a leader of the Gaullist RPR party of President Jacques Chirac, has predicted the plan would attract more foreigners to France and bolster the extreme right.

"Sans papiers" ("without papers") protesters, many of them are Malians who have lived in France for years, say they were deprived of residence rights by a stiffening of immigration laws in 1993 and are in a legal limbo as they can neither obtain residence rights nor be expelled for a variety of reasons -- including having children born in France.

The move seemed bound to raise an outcry on the right. Opinion polls show most voters want the hardline legislation enacted by former right-wing interior ministers Charles Pasqua and Jean-Louis Debre to stay.

The issue sparked nationwide controversy last August when police stormed a Paris church and forcibly evicted some 200 Africans who had taken refuge there to avoid expulsion. Magistrates later overturned orders expelling most of them.
There are an estimated five million foreigners in France, of whom about one million, mostly North Africans, are thought to be illegal.
